claims.source: These three loci are known to have brain-specific (Ahrens et al., 2012), lens-specific (Posner et al., 2017), and ubiquitous (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) expression, respectively, in teleost fish (including zebrafish and medaka).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Posner et al., 2017.

claims.claim: ACTB2 has ubiquitous expression in teleost fish.
claims.source: These three loci are known to have brain-specific (Ahrens et al., 2012), lens-specific (Posner et al., 2017), and ubiquitous (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) expression, respectively, in teleost fish (including zebrafish and medaka).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in the developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos.
claims.source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in the lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos.
claims.source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos.
claims.source: We observed Venus fluorescent protein expression in the expected tissues: developing brain for ELAVL3-targeted embryos (Figure 1B), lens of the eye for CRYAA-targeted embryos (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and in all cells of the embryo for ACTB2-targeted embryos (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: Supported by visual observation and shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In all embryos screened, Venus expression was not observed in a tissue that was not specifically targeted.
claims.source: In all embryos screened, we did not observe Venus expression in a tissue that was not specifically targeted.
claims.evidence: This is a negative result reported from the screening.

claims.claim: Venus fluorescence was observed in over 40% of developed embryos for all three targeted loci.
claims.source: For all three targeted loci, we observed Venus fluorescence (suggestive of successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in) in over 40% of developed embryos (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The highest CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency at the ELAVL3 locus was achieved using both a chemically modified dsDNA HDR template and a small molecule HDR enhancer.
claims.source: For the ELAVL3 locus, we achieved the highest CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency using both a chemically modified dsDNA HDR template (i.e. IDT's Alt-R HDR Donor Blocks, see Methods) and a small molecule HDR enhancer as compared to an unmodified dsDNA HDR template (i.e. IDT's gBlocks, see Methods) and no small molecule HDR enhancer (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: No significant differences in lethality were observed between embryos injected with CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in reagents and non-injected wildtype embryos.
claims.source: We did not observe significant differences in the lethality of embryos injected with CRISPR/Cas9 knock-in reagents (including chemically modified dsDNA HDR template and/or small molecule HDR enhancer) compared to non-injected wildtype embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by lethality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claims.claim: The lethality of killifish embryos in the first two weeks of development is variable, whether injected or not.
claims.source: In general, the lethality of killifish embryos, whether injected or not, was variable in the first two weeks of development (dependent on breeders and clutch; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by lethality data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claims.claim: Injecting ~100 embryos per line is recommended to ensure successful generation of transgenic animals that survive past development.
claims.source: Thus, to ensure successful generation of transgenic animals that survive past development, we recommend injecting ~100 embryos per line.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed data.

claims.claim: The genomic knock-in occurred at the expected genomic locus as confirmed by PCR genotyping.
claims.source: Importantly, we confirmed that the genomic knock-in occurred at the expected genomic locus by PCR genotyping of DNA extracted from tail clips of the injected individuals (F0 founders) using 3 primers, 2 surrounding the insertion site for each gene and 1 in the Venus transgene (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 3; see below for sequencing confirmation in the F1 generation).
claims.evidence: Supported by PCR genotyping data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching.
claims.source: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching, consistent with what has been observed for ACTB2 knock-in in medaka (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) and perhaps due to the sensitivity of actin assembly to any perturbation (e.g. additional amino acids due to cleavage of the P2A peptide).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experiments, with comparison to medaka data cited from Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The sensitivity of actin assembly to perturbation may explain why ACTB2 knock-in embryos did not survive hatching.
claims.source: Knock-in at the ACTB2 locus resulted in Venus positive embryos that did not survive hatching, consistent with what has been observed for ACTB2 knock-in in medaka (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018) and perhaps due to the sensitivity of actin assembly to any perturbation (e.g. additional amino acids due to cleavage of the P2A peptide).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed lethality.

claims.claim: It may be more difficult to use this knock-in approach to generate stable lines targeting essential genes encoding proteins involved in sensitive assemblies such as ACTB2.
claims.source: Hence, this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in method allows for precise and efficient editing at several loci, including tissue-specific ones; however, it may be more difficult to use this knock-in approach to generate stable lines targeting essential genes encoding proteins involved in sensitive assemblies such as ACTB2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the ACTB2 lethality observation.

claims.claim: 67% of F0 founders produced Venus-positive F1 progeny when crossed with wildtype fish.
claims.source: Sixty-seven percent of F0 founders, when crossed with wildtype fish, produced Venus-positive F1 progeny (Figure 2A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by germline transmission data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claims.claim: 85% of F1 Venus-positive progeny from inter-crossing two Venus-positive F0 individuals were homozygous for the insertion at the ELAVL3 locus.
claims.source: Upon inter-crossing these founders, we found that 85% of the resulting F1 Venus-positive progeny were homozygous for the insertion at the ELAVL3 locus (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: Supported by genotyping data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the ELAVL3 locus was single copy and in frame, with no observed mutations within 1 kb around the insertion site.
claims.source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the ELAVL3 locus was as designed—single copy and in frame, with no observed mutations within 1 kb around the insertion site (Figure 1E; Figure 2A, C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1E, Figure 2A, C, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals showed no off-target editing at the three most likely off-target sites.
claims.source: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals at the three most likely off-target sites [predicted by CHOPCHOP (Labun et al., 2019)] showed no off-target editing at these sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Backcrossing founders to wildtype animals is recommended to limit the risk of off-target editing.
claims.source: Nevertheless, to limit the risk of off-target editing, we recommend backcrossing founders to wildtype animals.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the potential risk of off-target editing.

claims.claim: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord.
claims.source: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord (Figure 2E; anti-GFP staining), which is expected given that the ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish (Ahrens et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E and citation to Ahrens et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish.
claims.source: At the larval stage, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F1 homozygous individuals exhibit specific and strong Venus expression throughout the nervous system including the retina, brain, and spinal cord (Figure 2E; anti-GFP staining), which is expected given that the ELAVL3 promoter is commonly used as a pan-neuronal promoter in larval zebrafish (Ahrens et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Ahrens et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In adults, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F3 heterozygous individuals show strong Venus expression in the brain.
claims.source: In adults, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus F3 heterozygous individuals show strong Venus expression in the brain (Figure 2F) (while we did not specifically test retina and spinal cord in adults, Venus expression should also occur in these areas).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The Venus transcript colocalizes to the same brain regions and cells as the ELAVL3 transcript in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line.
claims.source: In situ hybridization indicates that the Venus transcript indeed colocalizes to the same brain regions and cells as the ELAVL3 transcript (Figure 2F; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The ELAVL3 transcript expression pattern in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line is consistent with that of ELAVL3 in wildtype animals.
claims.source: The ELAVL3 transcript expression pattern in the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus line is consistent with that of ELAVL3 in wildtype animals (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2G.

claims.claim: The knocked-in Venus transgene recapitulates the endogenous expression pattern of the targeted ELAVL3 locus in the brain.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that the knocked-in Venus transgene recapitulates the endogenous expression pattern of the targeted ELAVL3 locus in the brain.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization data.

claims.claim: A large increase in expression of Venus was observed in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals.
claims.source: As expected, we observed a large increase in expression of Venus in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals (with highest expression of Venus in homozygous animals; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: ELAVL3 expression level was not significantly different between animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype siblings.
claims.source: ELAVL3 expression level was not significantly different between animals heterozygous or homozygous for the ELAVL3-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype siblings (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C; although there might be a slight, non-significant reduction in the homozygous mutants).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Inserting a fluorescent protein gene at the endogenous ELAVL3 locus does not significantly impair the expression of the endogenous gene.
claims.source: Thus, inserting a fluorescent protein gene at the endogenous ELAVL3 locus does not significantly impair the expression of the endogenous gene.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the RT-qPCR data.

claims.claim: The knock-in method enables generation of stable lines of transgenic vertebrate animals in 2–3 months.
claims.source: Collectively, these observations indicate that the knock-in method we developed enables generation of stable lines of transgenic vertebrate animals in 2–3 months.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the timeline of the experiments.

claims.claim: Successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of a 2 kb long insertion sequence was observed in ~50% of developed embryos.
claims.source: We observed successful CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of this longer sequence in ~50% of developed embryos (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Supported by efficiency data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: There was no decrease in efficiency or change in embryo lethality for the 2 kb insertion relative to the shorter 0.8 kb insertion at the ELAVL3 locus.
claims.source: There was no decrease in efficiency or change in embryo lethality for this longer insertion relative to the shorter (0.8 kb) insertion previously tested at the same locus (Figure 3B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparative data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claims.claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet integration at the ELAVL3 locus was the expected size and in frame without mutations.
claims.source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet integration at the ELAVL3 locus was the expected size and in frame without mutations (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet animals showed no off-target editing at the three predicted most likely off-target sites.
claims.source: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of homozygous F1 animals at the three predicted most likely off-target sites showed no off-target editing in these fish (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Imaging coronal brain sections of adult F0 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish showed cells expressing both oScarlet and Venus.
claims.source: Imaging coronal brain sections of adult F0 ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish showed cells expressing both oScarlet and Venus (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: oScarlet expression was confined to nuclei while Venus expression was seen in both cell bodies and projections in ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish.
claims.source: As expected, oScarlet expression was confined to nuclei while Venus expression was seen in both cell bodies and projections (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Imaging the whole brain of adult ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish revealed oScarlet-positive nuclei throughout the brain.
claims.source: Imaging the whole brain of adult ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet killifish revealed oScarlet-positive nuclei throughout the brain (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: This method allows for pan-neuronal expression in the adult brain and could be leveraged to drive expression of molecular tools in a neuronal-specific manner.
claims.source: Thus, this method allows for pan-neuronal expression in the adult brain and could be leveraged to drive expression of molecular tools e.g. the optogenetic ion channel channelrhodopsin [~1 kb] (Boyden et al., 2005) or the genetically encoded calcium indicator GCaMP [~1.3 kb] (Ahrens et al., 2012) in a neuronal-specific manner.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about potential applications based on the demonstrated capability.

claims.claim: NPY and HCRT neuronal populations are critical for organismal homeostasis through modulation of behaviors, including feeding behavior and sleep-wake behavior.
claims.source: These neuronal populations are critical for organismal homeostasis through modulation of behaviors, including feeding behavior (Jeong et al., 2018) and sleep-wake behavior (Chiu and Prober, 2013; Prober et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Jeong et al., 2018; Chiu and Prober, 2013; Prober et al., 2006; and Singh et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Growing evidence suggests that NPY and HCRT neuronal populations may be altered with age.
claims.source: Growing evidence also suggests that these neuronal populations may be altered with age (Fronczek et al., 2012; Hunt et al., 2015; Li et al., 2022; Montesano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Fronczek et al., 2012; Hunt et al., 2015; Li et al., 2022; and Montesano et al., 2019.

claims.claim: PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the NPY or HCRT locus was single-copy and in frame at the targeted genomic location.
claims.source: PCR amplification and genotyping by Sanger sequencing of F1 animals confirmed that the T2A-Venus integration at the NPY or HCRT locus was as designed—single-copy and in frame at the targeted genomic location (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Imaging of coronal brain sections of the adult HCRT-T2A-Venus killifish line showed a dense and isolated population of Venus-positive cell bodies in the dorsal periventricular hypothalamus.
claims.source: Imaging of coronal brain sections of the adult HCRT-T2A-Venus killifish line showed a dense and isolated population of Venus-positive cell bodies in the dorsal periventricular hypothalamus (Hd; homologous to the mammalian arcuate nucleus; Figure 4B), consistent with endogenous HCRT expression previously reported in the adult killifish brain (D'angelo, 2013; Montesano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and citations to D'angelo, 2013 and Montesano et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The adult NPY-T2A-Venus line exhibited Venus-positive cell bodies throughout the brain, including in the central posterior thalamic nucleus, anterior tuberal nucleus, periventricular and lateral hypothalamus, and periventricular gray zone of the optic tectum.
claims.source: In contrast, the adult NPY-T2A-Venus line exhibited Venus-positive cell bodies throughout the brain, including in the central posterior thalamic nucleus (CP), anterior tuberal nucleus (TNa), periventricular and lateral hypothalamus, as well as in the periventricular gray zone (PGZ) of the optic tectum (OT) (Figure 4D), consistent with endogenous NPY expression previously reported in the adult killifish brain (D'angelo, 2013; Montesano et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D and citations to D'angelo, 2013 and Montesano et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Venus transcript co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line.
claims.source: Using in situ hybridization, we verified that Venus transcript indeed co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5) or the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Venus transcript co-localized with the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line.
claims.source: Using in situ hybridization, we verified that Venus transcript indeed co-localized with the HCRT transcript in the HCRT-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 5) or the NPY transcript in the NPY-T2A-Venus line (Figure 4E; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The Venus expression profiles observed in the NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines were consistent with those of endogenous NPY and HCRT transcripts, respectively, in wildtype animals.
claims.source: The Venus expression profiles observed in the NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines were consistent with those of endogenous NPY and HCRT transcripts, respectively, in wildtype animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparison of in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A large increase in expression of Venus was observed in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals.
claims.source: As expected, we observed a large increase in expression of Venus in animals heterozygous or homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele compared to wildtype animals (with highest expression of Venus in homozygous animals; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: In animals heterozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was similar to that of wildtype animals.
claims.source: In animals heterozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was similar to that of wildtype animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: In animals homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was slightly but significantly lower compared to wildtype siblings.
claims.source: However, in animals homozygous for the NPY-T2A-Venus allele, NPY expression level was slightly but significantly lower compared to wildtype siblings (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The presence of the transgene at homozygous levels slightly impairs expression of endogenous NPY.
claims.source: These observations suggest that the presence of the transgene at homozygous levels slightly impairs expression of endogenous NPY.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the RT-qPCR data.

claims.claim: Use of heterozygous animals with edited alleles may be more conservative to preserve robust expression of the endogenous locus.
claims.source: Thus, in this case (and likely in other cases), use of heterozygous animals with edited alleles may be more conservative to preserve robust expression of the endogenous locus.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation based on the NPY expression data.

claims.claim: The observation that the expression pattern of Venus recapitulates that of the targeted endogenous gene for all genes targeted supports the notion that in-frame off-target insertions are rare with this method.
claims.source: The observation that the expression pattern of Venus recapitulates that of the targeted endogenous gene for all genes targeted here also supports the notion that in-frame off-target insertions are rare with this method.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern data.

claims.claim: The generation of NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines serves as proof of principle that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in is a powerful method in killifish to drive cell-type-specific expression.
claims.source: The generation of these lines serves as proof of principle that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in is a powerful method in killifish to drive cell-type-specific expression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the successful generation of cell-type-specific lines.

claims.claim: These neuron-specific lines should help the development of the killifish for systems neuroscience studies.
claims.source: These neuron-specific lines should also help the development of the killifish for systems neuroscience studies.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about future applications.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of large inserts was observed at five distinct genomic loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, ACTB2, NPY, and HCRT), with >40% efficiency at tested loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, and ACTB2).
claims.source: We observe CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of large inserts at five distinct genomic loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, ACTB2, NPY, and HCRT), with >40% efficiency at tested loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, and ACTB2).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental results.

claims.claim: With this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach, a >65% germline transmission rate was observed for knock-in at the ELAVL3 locus.
claims.source: With this CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approach, we observe a >65% germline transmission rate for knock-in at the ELAVL3 locus.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the germline transmission data.

claims.claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency and germline transmission rates may vary depending on the genomic locus being targeted.
claims.source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in efficiency and germline transmission rates may vary depending on the genomic locus being targeted (Hsu et al., 2013; Labun et al., 2019), which might be due to the chromatin accessibility of that locus.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2013 and Labun et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Four stable knock-in lines were generated in this work: ELAVL3-T2A-Venus, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet, NPY-T2A-Venus, and HCRT-T2A-Venus.
claims.source: We have generated four stable knock-in lines in this work: ELAVL3-T2A-Venus, ELAVL3-T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet, NPY-T2A-Venus, and HCRT-T2A-Venus.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the lines generated.

claims.claim: The high efficiency of germline transmission observed in killifish may be due to the relatively slow rate of early cell division after fertilization in the African turquoise killifish.
claims.source: The high efficiency of germline transmission we observe in killifish may be due to the relatively slow rate of early cell division after fertilization in the African turquoise killifish (~4 times slower in this species relative to non-annual teleost fishes; Dolfi et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Dolfi et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The killifish model allows for easy and high-throughput injection of genome-editing machinery into embryos.
claims.source: The killifish model, with hundreds of embryos produced at a given time (for example using harem breeding), allows for easy and high-throughput injection of genome-editing machinery into embryos (Harel et al., 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Polačik et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Harel et al., 2015; Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; and Polačik et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The development of rapid and efficient knock-in establishes the killifish as a system for precise genetic engineering at scale.
claims.source: The development of rapid and efficient knock-in establishes the killifish as a system for precise genetic engineering at scale, which has been challenging so far in vertebrates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstrated capabilities.

claims.claim: Knock-in was first reported for short insertions (~8 bp) in killifish, though germline transmission of these inserts was not achieved.
claims.source: Knock-in was first reported for short insertions (~8 bp; though germline transmission of these inserts was not achieved) (Harel et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Harel et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Longer CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in insertions (~1 kb) were achieved in killifish (in F0 individuals) with 18–30% efficiency, though germline transmission was not shown.
claims.source: More recently, longer CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in insertions (~1 kb) were achieved in killifish (in F0 individuals) with 18–30% efficiency, though germline transmission was not shown (Oginuma et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Oginuma et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Knock-in of a long (1.5 kb) insertion was achieved for a specific locus with ~11% efficiency and successful germline transmission.
claims.source: Moreover, knock-in of a long (1.5 kb) insertion was achieved for a specific locus with ~11% efficiency and successful germline transmission (germline transmission rate not shown) (Krug et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Krug et al., 2023.

claims.claim: The knock-in method developed here uses reagents that are commercially available, eliminating the need for cloning and PCR.
claims.source: The knock-in method developed here uses reagents that are commercially available, eliminating the need for cloning and PCR and making this method easy to adopt.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claims.claim: The steps described here could serve as a blueprint for knock-in approaches in other emerging model organisms.
claims.source: Together, the steps described here could serve as a blueprint for knock-in approaches in other emerging model organisms.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about broader applications.

claims.claim: High insertion efficiencies (>40%) and germline transmission have been achieved with different CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in methods in teleost fish.
claims.source: While it is difficult without side-by-side experiments to compare each knock-in approach, high insertion efficiencies (>40%) and germline transmission have been achieved with different methods, for example, in zebrafish using plasmid donors with in vivo linearization and short homology arms (Wierson et al., 2020), in medaka using dsDNA PCR product donors, biotin modification and short homology arms (Seleit et al., 2021), and (reported here) in killifish using synthetic dsDNA donors, IDT's proprietary modification (Alt-R HDR Donor Block) and middle-range length (150–200 bp) homology arms.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Wierson et al., 2020 and Seleit et al., 2021, and data from this study.

claims.claim: A variety of approaches for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in have been successful in teleost fish, expanding the toolkit that can be used in these species.
claims.source: Thus, a variety of approaches for CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in have been successful in teleost fish, expanding the toolkit that can be used in these species.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of different methods.

claims.claim: The use of synthetic, chemically-modified repair templates with ~150–200 bp homology arms has the advantage of being easily adoptable without expertise in molecular biology techniques.
claims.source: Our method uses synthetic, chemically-modified repair templates with ~150–200 bp homology arms, which has the advantage of being easily adoptable without expertise in molecular biology techniques (cloning or PCR).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the method's advantages.

claims.claim: There is no preparation required for reagents in this method, which helps save hands-on time.

results.result: The African turquoise killifish is characterized as a powerful vertebrate model system with rapid sexual maturity (3-4 weeks), compressed lifespan (4-6 months), and the shortest generation time of laboratory-bred vertebrates (2 months).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Hu and Brunet, 2018; Kim et al., 2016; Polačik et al., 2016). These are background claims about the model system that provide context for the study.

results.result: The killifish has an established genetic toolkit including a sequenced genome, Tol2 transgenesis, CRISPR/Cas9 knock-out, and CRISPR/Cas13 knock-down, which has enabled discoveries in aging, regeneration, evolution, development, and embryonic diapause.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C14 are supported by multiple citations to prior work. These are background claims establishing the existing state of the field and providing rationale for the current study's contribution.

results.result: The authors designed a CRISPR/Cas9-mediated HDR approach using chemically modified dsDNA templates with 150-200 bp homology arms, positioned 2-7 bp from Cas9 cut sites, incorporating T2A self-cleaving peptides to avoid direct protein fusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 describe the methodological design, which is clearly documented with rationale (C15 cites Auer et al., 2014 for the problem being addressed; C17 references IDT recommendations). The design is appropriate and well-justified.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in achieved tissue-specific Venus expression in over 40% of developed embryos at three loci (ELAVL3, CRYAA, ACTB2), with fluorescence observed in expected tissues (brain, lens, ubiquitous) and no off-target tissue expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C27 are supported by visual data (Figure 1B, 1C) and citations establishing expected expression patterns. The >40% efficiency is quantified and the tissue specificity is demonstrated both positively (C23-C25) and negatively (C26). This represents a core finding of the study.

results.result: Chemically modified dsDNA HDR templates combined with small molecule HDR enhancers achieved the highest knock-in efficiency at the ELAVL3 locus without significantly increasing embryo lethality, though embryo survival is variable and ~100 embryos per line are recommended.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by comparative data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C. The statistical comparison shows significance (p=0.03 in C28), and lethality data shows no significant differences between conditions. C31 is a reasonable recommendation based on the observed variability.

results.result: PCR genotyping confirmed knock-in at expected genomic loci, though ACTB2 knock-in embryos did not survive hatching, consistent with medaka observations and potentially due to actin assembly sensitivity, suggesting limitations for targeting essential genes in sensitive protein assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by PCR data (Figure 1D) and comparison to prior work (Gutierrez-Triana et al., 2018). C34 is speculative but reasonable, and C35 is an appropriate inference about method limitations based on the ACTB2 result.

results.result: 67% of F0 founders transmitted Venus-positive progeny to F1, with 85% of F1 progeny from F0×F0 crosses being homozygous. Sanger sequencing confirmed single-copy, in-frame integration without mutations within 1 kb or at predicted off-target sites, though backcrossing is recommended.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are well-supported by germline transmission data (Figure 2A-B), genotyping (Figure 2C-D), and sequencing data (Figure 1E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1-2). The off-target analysis (C39) is thorough for the three most likely sites. C40 is a prudent recommendation despite negative off-target results.

results.result: ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals exhibit Venus expression throughout the nervous system at larval and adult stages, with Venus transcript colocalizing with endogenous ELAVL3 transcript, demonstrating that the knocked-in transgene recapitulates endogenous expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C46 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 2E-F) and in situ hybridization data (Figure 2F-G). The colocalization and consistency with wildtype patterns provide strong evidence that the transgene faithfully reports endogenous expression. C42 provides appropriate context from zebrafish literature.

results.result: RT-qPCR analysis showed large increases in Venus expression in ELAVL3-T2A-Venus animals without significantly impairing endogenous ELAVL3 expression, and the method enables generation of stable transgenic lines in 2-3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B-C). The lack of significant difference in ELAVL3 expression (C48) is important for validating that the knock-in doesn't disrupt endogenous function. C50 is a reasonable summary of the timeline demonstrated in the study.

results.result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in successfully inserted a 2 kb sequence (T2A-Venus-P2A-H2B-oScarlet) at the ELAVL3 locus with ~50% efficiency and no decrease compared to shorter insertions, producing pan-neuronal expression with proper subcellular localization that could be leveraged for molecular tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 are supported by efficiency data (Figure 3B), sequencing (Figure 3C), off-target analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and imaging data (Figure 3D-E). The demonstration of longer insertions without efficiency loss is significant. C58 is a reasonable inference about potential applications based on the demonstrated capability.

results.result: NPY-T2A-Venus and HCRT-T2A-Venus lines were generated with cell-type-specific expression patterns consistent with endogenous neuropeptide expression, targeting neuronal populations critical for homeostasis and potentially altered with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C66 are supported by citations for background (C59-C60), sequencing data (C61, Figure 4A), imaging (C62-C63, Figure 4B, D), and in situ hybridization (C64-C66, Figure 4C, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The expression patterns match expected endogenous patterns, validating the approach for cell-type-specific targeting.

results.result: RT-qPCR analysis of NPY-T2A-Venus animals showed that heterozygous animals maintain normal NPY expression while homozygous animals show slightly but significantly reduced NPY expression, suggesting heterozygous animals may be preferable to preserve robust endogenous expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The statistical significance of reduced NPY expression in homozygotes (C69, p=0.003) is clearly demonstrated. C70-C71 are reasonable inferences and recommendations based on this data, providing important guidance for users of the method.

results.result: The consistent recapitulation of endogenous expression patterns across all targeted genes supports that in-frame off-target insertions are rare, establishing CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in as a powerful method for cell-type-specific expression in killifish with potential applications in systems neuroscience.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are reasonable inferences based on the cumulative evidence from multiple loci. C74 is speculative about future applications but appropriately qualified. The logic that consistent on-target expression patterns argue against frequent off-target insertions is sound.

results.result: The study achieved CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in at five loci with >40% efficiency and >65% germline transmission, generating four stable lines and establishing killifish as a system for precise genetic engineering at scale, potentially facilitated by slow early cell division and high-throughput embryo production.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C81 are supported by the cumulative data from the study. C77 and C79 are speculative but supported by citations. C80-C81 are reasonable conclusions about the significance of the work. These claims effectively summarize the major achievements and implications of the study.

results.result: The current method improves upon prior killifish knock-in approaches (8 bp without germline transmission, ~1 kb at 18-30% without germline transmission shown, 1.5 kb at ~11%) by using commercially available reagents without cloning or PCR, potentially serving as a blueprint for other organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by citations to prior work (Harel et al., 2015; Oginuma et al., 2022; Krug et al., 2023). The comparison appropriately contextualizes the current work's improvements. C85-C86 accurately describe advantages and potential broader impact.

results.result: Multiple CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in approaches have achieved >40% efficiency in teleost fish using different strategies. The synthetic dsDNA approach offers advantages of ease of adoption and no reagent preparation but has limitations in template length (≤3000 bp), complexity, wait time, and cost.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 are supported by citations (Wierson et al., 2020; Seleit et al., 2021) and accurately describe the advantages (C89-C91) and limitations (C92) of the method. C93-C94 provide reasonable practical recommendations based on these trade-offs.

results.result: The knock-in method should enable studies of complex phenotypes including aging and disease, potentially allowing generation of scalable human disease models that integrate genetics and age as risk factors, which could identify new treatment strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are speculative about future applications. While C97 is supported by citations about mouse models, C95-C96 and C98 are forward-looking statements about potential applications that have not been demonstrated in this study. These represent reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support.

results.result: The study demonstrates the power of knock-in with self-cleaving peptides for cell-type-specific expression of molecular tools, which should enable studies in systems neuroscience and other fields. Additional variations like landing pads and inducible promoters could further complete the toolkit.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 appropriately summarize the study's contributions (C99) and speculate about future applications and developments (C100-C102). C101 is supported by citations (Soriano, 1999; Gossen and Bujard, 1992; Gossen et al., 1995). These are reasonable forward-looking statements based on demonstrated capabilities.

results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 describe standard husbandry methods supported by citations to established guidelines (Astre et al., 2022b; Bedbrook et al., 2023; Nath et al., 2023; Reichard et al., 2022; Žák et al., 2020). These are methodological details necessary for reproducibility.
